entry: American conservative cable news channel, based in [[New York City]] and owned by Fox Corporation. Created in 1996 by [[Rupert Murdoch]] to appeal to a conservative audience, it was the most-watched cable news network in the United States as of 2022. Its audience skews heavily Republican and older. Critics argue that the channel has broadcast biased and false reporting in favor of the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] and its politicians, including false claims of fraud by Dominion voting machines in its 2020 presidential election coverage. In 2023 it settled a defamation case with Dominion Voting Systems for $787 million.

Omnivorous mammal of several genera in the family [[Canidae]]. Foxes have a flattened skull, upright triangular ears, a pointed snout and a long bushy tail. 12 species belong to the "true fox" genus *Vulpes*, and about 25 other current or extinct species are sometimes also called foxes. Foxes live on every continent except Antarctica. The most common and widespread species is the [[Red fox|red fox]], with about 47 recognized subspecies; in the largest species, males weigh between 4.1 and 8.7 kg. The smallest, the [[Fennec fox]], weighs 0.7 to 1.6 kg. Their reputation for cunning has made foxes prominent in [[Folklore|folklore]] worldwide. Hunting foxes with packs of hounds, long established in Europe and especially the [[British Isles]], was exported by European settlers to the [[New World]].

Taiwanese multinational electronics contract manufacturer, the world's largest of its kind. Founded in 1974 as Hon Hai Precision Industry, it is headquartered in New Taipei City, [[Taiwan]], but earns most of its revenue in China. It manufactures products for [[Sony]], [[Nintendo]], [[Microsoft]] and [[Cisco]], and makes the [[IPhone|iPhone]] and iPad. As of 2012 its factories made an estimated 40% of all consumer electronics sold worldwide. In 2019 Young Liu succeeded founder Terry Gou as chairman, a handover analysts said pointed the company toward [[Semiconductor|semiconductors]], artificial intelligence and robotics. Its Chinese plants have faced allegations of excessive overtime and safety lapses.

Polish composer and pianist of the early Romantic period, who wrote primarily for solo piano. Born in Żelazowa Wola and raised in [[Warsaw]], he left Poland shortly before the November 1830 Uprising and settled in [[Paris]]. He gave only 30 public performances, preferring the intimacy of the salon, and supported himself by teaching and publishing. He formed a friendship with [[Franz Liszt]] and was admired by [[Robert Schumann]]. All his compositions feature the piano, including mazurkas, waltzes, [[Nocturnes (Chopin)|nocturnes]], polonaises, études and sonatas. His works drew on Polish folk music and on the models of [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart|Mozart]] and [[Franz Schubert|Schubert]]. His innovations in style, harmony and form were influential throughout and after the late Romantic period.

Geometric shape or set with detailed structure at arbitrarily small scales. Fractals are typically self-similar, with parts resembling the whole, and their fractal dimension strictly exceeds their topological dimension. Doubling the edge lengths of a filled polygon multiplies its area by four, but a fractal's content scales by a power that is generally not an integer. The term was coined in 1975 by [[Benoit Mandelbrot|Benoît Mandelbrot]] from Latin *frāctus*, meaning "broken". Examples include the [[Mandelbrot set]], the Koch snowflake and the Sierpinski triangle. Fractals appear in most [[Chaos theory|chaotic]] processes, and in nature, art and architecture.

Abstract [[Coordinate system|coordinate system]], with an origin, orientation and scale specified in physical space, used to describe position and motion. A frame is defined by reference points identified both mathematically, by coordinate values, and physically, by markers. An inertial frame is one in which Newton's first law holds: an object at rest stays at rest, and one moving at constant velocity continues so, unless a force acts on it. Non-inertial frames, such as one fixed to Earth's surface, require fictitious forces like the [[Coriolis force]] and [[Centrifugal force|centrifugal force]] to explain observations. According to [[Special relativity]], the laws of physics and the speed of light are the same in all inertial frames, so time belongs to a frame rather than being absolute. [[General relativity]] extended the framework to non-inertial frames by describing gravity as the curvature of spacetime.

Haitian physician and dictator who served as president of Haiti from 1957 to 1971. Known as Papa Doc, he was elected in 1957 on a populist and [[Nationalism|black nationalist]] platform. After thwarting a military coup in July 1958, his regime became increasingly autocratic. In 1964 he declared himself president for life after a sham referendum. His secret police, the *Tonton Macoute*, tortured or killed opponents; it grew to 300,000 members, and more than half the government budget went to it and the Presidential Guard. An estimated 40,000 deaths were attributed to his security apparatus. He promoted [[Haitian Vodou|Vodou]] as part of a personality cult, and was succeeded by his son, Jean-Claude.

French Socialist politician, president of France from 1981 to 1995. He was the first left-wing president of the Fifth Republic and the longest-serving republican head of state in French history. His first government nationalized key firms, introduced a 39-hour week and abolished the death penalty, but it soon turned to austerity and market liberalization. Twice forced into "cohabitation" with conservative governments, he worked with [[Helmut Kohl]] to advance [[European integration]] through the Maastricht Treaty, and accepted [[German reunification]]. In 1985 his government ordered the bombing of the Greenpeace ship *Rainbow Warrior* in [[Auckland]]. He had concealed [[Prostate cancer|prostate cancer]] for most of his presidency.

French Renaissance writer, physician and [[Humanism|humanist]], best known for the satirical novels *Gargantua and Pantagruel*. Called the first great French prose author, he was a Greek scholar and a Christian humanist who admired [[Erasmus]]. Trained as a Franciscan and then a Benedictine monk, he studied medicine and in 1532 moved to [[Lyon]], where he practiced at the Hôtel-Dieu hospital. The first two books tell the childhoods of the giants Gargantua and Pantagruel; the Third and Fourth Books are more erudite. He criticized medieval scholasticism and lampooned the abuses of princes and popes, drawing opposition from [[John Calvin]] and the Catholic hierarchy. The adjective *Rabelaisian* describes work marked by gross, robust humor and bold caricature.

French filmmaker, critic and actor, a founder of the French New Wave. Writing for *Cahiers du Cinéma* under André Bazin, he promoted the auteur theory, which holds that a film's director is its true author. His debut feature, *The 400 Blows* (1959), starring Jean-Pierre Léaud as Antoine Doinel, defined the New Wave, and Doinel's story continued in later films. Other notable works include *Shoot the Piano Player* (1960), *Jules and Jim* (1962) and *Day for Night* (1973), which won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. He wrote *Hitchcock/Truffaut* (1966), a book-length interview with [[Alfred Hitchcock]]. He also acted in other directors' films, including Steven Spielberg's *Close Encounters of the Third Kind*.

Best known French poet of the late [[Middle Ages]], whose work draws on his own brushes with the law. Born in [[Paris]] and raised by a foster father, Guillaume de Villon, a chaplain and professor of canon law, he took the surname Villon from him. He earned a bachelor's degree from the University of Paris in 1449 and a master's in 1452. In 1455 a street brawl left a priest dead, and Villon fled; he was pardoned in 1456. Around Christmas 1456 the chapel of the Collège de Navarre was robbed of 500 gold crowns, and Villon was implicated. His poems, especially *Le Testament*, are read as partly autobiographical and include the "Ballade des pendus" on the fate of hanged criminals.

American actress and film producer. She has won three [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]] for Best Actress, for *Fargo* (1996), *Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri* (2017) and *Nomadland* (2020), making her the second woman to win that award three times after [[Katharine Hepburn]]. She also produced *Nomadland*, which won Best Picture, making her the first person to win Academy Awards as both producer and performer for the same film. She has been married to filmmaker [[Coen brothers|Joel Coen]] since 1984. She won a Tony Award for *Good People* (2011) and a Primetime Emmy for the [[HBO]] miniseries *Olive Kitteridge*.

Kingdom of the [[Franks]], c. 481–843, the largest post-Roman kingdom in Western Europe. Under [[Clovis I]], who conquered Soissons in 486 and Aquitaine in 507, the Franks unified most of Gaul and founded the [[Merovingian dynasty]]. The Carolingian dynasty, through Pepin the Short and [[Charlemagne]], secured the realm's greatest expansion. Charlemagne was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 800, creating the [[Carolingian Empire]], which extended from the Pyrenees to the Elbe. Its lands were repeatedly divided among rulers, and the Treaty of Verdun in 843 split the realm into East Francia, West Francia and Middle Francia. West Francia became the [[Kingdom of France]] under the Capetians, and East Francia became the [[Kingdom of Germany]].

English philosopher and statesman, Lord Chancellor of England under James I. Often called the father of [[Empiricism|empiricism]], he argued that scientific knowledge should rest on inductive reasoning and careful observation of nature. He proposed a skeptical, methodical approach that would help scientists avoid misleading themselves, and he is counted among the founders of the [[Scientific method]]. His ideas were influential throughout the [[Scientific Revolution]]. In 1597 [[Elizabeth I]] appointed him her legal adviser, the first recipient of the Queen's counsel designation. After his impeachment for corruption, he was briefly imprisoned and barred from public office. A fringe theory, first proposed in the mid-19th century, holds that he wrote some of the plays attributed to [[William Shakespeare]].

English molecular biologist, biophysicist and neuroscientist. With [[James Watson]], [[Rosalind Franklin]] and Maurice Wilkins, he helped decipher the helical structure of [[DNA]]. His and Watson's 1953 paper in *Nature* laid the groundwork for understanding DNA structure and function, and Crick, Watson and Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. He is widely known for the central dogma of [[Molecular biology|molecular biology]], which holds that once information passes from nucleic acids to proteins, it cannot flow back. Later, at the Salk Institute for Biological Studies in La Jolla, California, he turned to theoretical neurobiology and the scientific study of [[Consciousness|consciousness]].

English explorer and privateer. He completed the second circumnavigation of the world, the first by an English expedition, from 1577 to 1580 aboard the *Golden Hind*. Crossing the [[Pacific Ocean]], then an area of exclusive Spanish interest, he claimed New Albion on the North American coast and plundered Spanish ships and towns for treasure. [[Elizabeth I]] knighted him in 1581. Drake was second-in-command of the English fleet that repulsed the Spanish Armada in 1588. His privateering led the Spanish to brand him a pirate, known to them as *El Draque*. He died of [[Dysentery|dysentery]] after a failed assault on [[Panama]].

American film director, producer and screenwriter, a leading figure of [[New Hollywood]]. He directed *The Godfather* (1972) and *The Godfather Part II* (1974), both Best Picture winners; the second also won him Best Director. *The Conversation* (1974) and *Apocalypse Now* (1979) each won the Palme d'Or at the [[Cannes Film Festival]]. *Apocalypse Now*, a [[Vietnam War]] epic with a notoriously difficult production, made him one of only ten filmmakers to win the award twice. He later directed *The Outsiders*, *Bram Stoker's Dracula* and *The Rainmaker*, then turned to independent, experimental films. He founded American Zoetrope and later became a vintner in Napa, California. In 2024 he self-financed *Megalopolis*, which drew mixed reception; he was accused of sexual misconduct that year.

English polymath and originator of [[Eugenics|eugenics]], a term he coined in 1883. He produced over 340 papers and books across statistics, anthropology, psychology and meteorology. He developed the statistical concept of [[Correlation|correlation]] and promoted regression toward the mean, and was the first to apply statistical methods to human differences and the inheritance of intelligence. He popularized the phrase "nature versus nurture" and founded psychometrics. His method of classifying [[Fingerprint|fingerprints]] proved useful in forensic science, and he devised the first weather map. A half-cousin of [[Charles Darwin]], he has drawn significant criticism for his advocacy of eugenics, social Darwinism and biological racism.

Last Holy Roman Emperor, reigning from 1792 to 1806, and the first Emperor of Austria from 1804. Born in [[Florence]], the eldest son of Leopold II, he acceded while his empire was embroiled in the French Revolutionary Wars. When [[Napoleon]] crowned himself Emperor of the French, Francis assumed the title Emperor of Austria. After Napoleon created the Confederation of the Rhine, he abdicated as Holy Roman Emperor in 1806, in effect dissolving the [[Holy Roman Empire]]. He was forced to give his daughter Marie Louise to Napoleon in marriage. In 1813 he helped defeat Napoleon in the War of the Sixth Coalition. At the [[Congress of Vienna]], largely dominated by his chancellor [[Klemens von Metternich]], most of his ancient dominions were restored. Later viewed as a reactionary, he was succeeded by his son Ferdinand I of Austria.

King of France from 1515 to 1547, and a patron of the [[Renaissance]]. He succeeded Louis XII, who died without a legitimate son. He attracted Italian artists to his court, including [[Leonardo da Vinci]], whose *Mona Lisa* Francis had acquired. His reign saw the growth of central power, the spread of [[Protestantism|Protestantism]] and humanism, and the start of French exploration of the New World, when [[Jacques Cartier]] claimed lands in the Americas for France. For promoting the French language he became known as the "Father and Restorer of Letters". He unsuccessfully continued the [[Italian Wars]] against the [[Habsburg monarchy|Habsburgs]]. After being captured at the Battle of Pavia, he formed a Franco-Ottoman alliance with [[Suleiman the Magnificent]], a controversial move for a Christian king.

Navarrese cleric and missionary, co-founder of the [[Jesuits|Society of Jesus]]. A companion of [[Ignatius of Loyola]], he was one of the first seven Jesuits to take vows of poverty and chastity, in Paris in 1534. As a representative of the [[Portuguese Empire]] he undertook extensive missionary work across Asia, playing a major role in the evangelization of India, particularly at [[Goa]]. He led the first Christian mission to Japan and was the first major missionary to venture into [[Borneo]] and the [[Maluku Islands]]. He died on Shangchuan Island while trying to enter Ming China. Venerated as the Apostle of the Indies and Apostle of Japan, he was canonized in 1622. In 1927 Pope Pius XI named him, with [[Thérèse of Lisieux]], co-patron of all foreign missions.

Italian Catholic friar and mystic who founded the Franciscan Order. Born into a wealthy family in Assisi, he turned to a life of poverty and devotion, repairing chapels and caring for the sick. After a journey to Rome to meet [[Pope Innocent III]], he gained approval for the Order of Friars Minor, which grew rapidly under his leadership. Clare of Assisi, whom he met, founded the Poor Clares. In 1219 he traveled to Egypt to try to convert Sultan al-Kamil during the Fifth Crusade. He arranged the first live nativity scene, at Greccio, as part of the annual [[Christmas]] celebration. According to tradition, he displayed stigmata in 1224. Canonized in 1228, he is associated with the patronage of animals and [[Ecology|the environment]], and with Catherine of Siena is patron saint of Italy.

Spanish general and dictator who ruled Spain from 1939 to 1975. He led the Nationalist forces that overthrew the Second Spanish Republic in the [[Spanish Civil War]], and was appointed head of state in 1936. His regime, known as [[Francoist Spain]], used forced labor, concentration camps and executions, causing at least 30,000 deaths after the war, with some estimates exceeding 200,000. Spain stayed neutral in World War II but supported the [[Axis powers]]. From the late 1950s, technocratic, economically liberal policies produced rapid growth known as the "Spanish miracle", although the regime remained authoritarian. He built a [[Cult of personality|personality cult]] around his rule and restored the monarchy, and he was succeeded by [[Juan Carlos I|King Juan Carlos]], who led the transition to democracy.

Spanish painter and printmaker, often described as the last of the Old Masters and the first of the moderns. He is considered the most important Spanish artist of the late 18th and early 19th centuries. Appointed court painter to the Spanish Crown in 1786, he produced portraits of the aristocracy and royalty, along with [[Rococo]]-style tapestry designs. A severe illness in 1793 left him deaf, after which his work grew darker and more pessimistic. His prints *The Disasters of War*, published posthumously, and his 1814 paintings *The Second of May 1808* and *The Third of May 1808* reflect the [[Peninsular War]]. His Black Paintings, applied to the walls of his house, include *Saturn Devouring His Son*. In 1824 he left Spain for [[Bordeaux]], where he completed *La Tauromaquia*.

Central American statesman and military leader, president of the Federal Republic of Central America three times between 1829 and 1839. Born in [[Tegucigalpa]], he rose to prominence at the Battle of La Trinidad in 1827. He was also head of state of [[Honduras]] three times between 1827 and 1830, of [[El Salvador]] in 1832 and from 1839 to 1840, and of [[Costa Rica]], where he was captured and executed after trying to regain power. As a liberal reformer he enacted freedom of the press, of [[Freedom of speech|speech]] and of [[Freedom of religion|religion]], made marriage secular and abolished government-aided tithing. These reforms created powerful conservative enemies. After the federation fractured in 1837, conservatives led by Rafael Carrera divided Central America into five nations.
